extracted.intended_audience: patent office classifiers, patent examiners, patent information searchers, and other IP professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Authoritative guide to using and interpreting the International Patent Classification (IPC): how to compose and read classification symbols, hierarchical rules, presentation conventions, references/notes, Definitions, and supplementary material for classifying and searching patent documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary objectives of the IPC
rubrics_metrics.description: The Classification's primary purpose is the establishment of an effective search tool for retrieval of patent documents by IP offices and other users to establish novelty and evaluate inventive step/non-obviousness (including assessment of technical advance and utility) of technical disclosures in patent applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also serves to orderly arrange patent documents, provide a basis for selective dissemination, investigate state of the art, and prepare industrial property statistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Official language and publication
rubrics_metrics.description: The Classification is established in the English and French languages, both texts being equally authentic; Internet version on WIPO IPC website represents the official publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Official texts may be established in other languages per Article 3(2). The Internet version contains complete text of current and previous editions/versions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of classification symbols (layout)
rubrics_metrics.description: A complete classification symbol comprises the combined symbols representing the section, class, subclass and main group or subgroup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules for composition and examples are provided (e.g., section letter, two-digit class number, subclass letter, group number with oblique slash).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sections as highest hierarchical level
rubrics_metrics.description: Sections are the highest level of hierarchy of the Classification and are designated by capital letters A–H, each with a broad section title (e.g., A HUMAN NECESSITIES, H ELECTRICITY).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subsections may exist as informative headings without classification symbols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class symbol and title conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Class symbol = section letter + two-digit number; class title gives an indication of the class content; some classes may have an informative class index.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: H01 BASIC ELECTRIC ELEMENTS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subclass symbol and guidance headings
rubrics_metrics.description: Subclass symbol = class symbol + capital letter; subclass title indicates content precisely and subclasses may have an index and a Guidance Heading when a large part relates to common subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: H01S DEVICES USING STIMULATED EMISSION; Guidance Headings introduced where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Groups: main groups and subgroups numbering rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Each group symbol consists of subclass symbol followed by two numbers separated by an oblique slash. Main group symbol ends with '/00'; subgroups have numbers other than 00 and are ordered as if decimal expansions of the main group number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: H01S 3/00 (main group), H01S 3/02 (subgroup). Subgroups are ordered numerically (3/036 after 3/03 and before 3/04).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading subgroup titles and dependency
rubrics_metrics.description: A subgroup title is dependent upon and restricted by the titles of the groups under which it is indented; subgroup titles beginning with lowercase are continuations of the higher-level title; those that are complete expressions begin with a capital letter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The subgroup title must always be read in the context of its parent group's titles (examples given).

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of hierarchy (indentation/dots determine hierarchy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The IPC is hierarchical: contents of lower levels are subdivisions of higher levels. The hierarchy among subgroups is determined solely by the number of dots (level of indentation) preceding their titles, not by subgroup numbering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show three-dot subgroup being superior to a four-dot subgroup even if numeric lengths differ; dots are used in place of repeated higher-level titles to avoid redundancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Option to classify in main groups only
rubrics_metrics.description: Industrial property offices lacking sufficient expertise for detailed classification may classify in main groups only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is explicitly permitted as an option for offices with limited resources or expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of groups within a subclass
rubrics_metrics.description: Groups in each subclass are arranged to assist users; for newer subclasses, main groups are generally arranged from most complex/highly specialised to least complex/least specialised subject matter; residual main groups, when needed, are placed at the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'standardised sequence' facilitates searching and reflects subject-matter complexity/specialisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and function of Guidance Headings
rubrics_metrics.description: A guidance heading is a short underlined statement placed before the first of successive main groups relating to common subject matter indicating that commonality; it extends to the next guidance heading or a heavy line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In exceptional cases a guidance heading may be provided for a single main group; examples provided (e.g., 'Ploughs').

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation of titles (multipart titles and semicolons)
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles may indicate content via a single phrase or several related phrases linked together; multipart titles separated by semicolons should be interpreted as separate titles, each part being read independently as its own title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used when desirable to treat distinct subject-matter together that cannot be covered by a single phrase (examples given).

rubrics_metrics.name: References: phrase in brackets referring to other places
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles may contain bracketed phrases referring to another place in the Classification; such references show that the referred place covers the subject matter mentioned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References can serve various functions (limiting, precedence, application-oriented, informative, out of residual place); examples show placement and syntax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limiting references — scope-limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: A scope-limitation reference excludes specified subject matter from the scope of the place where it appears even if that subject matter would otherwise fulfil the place's definition, and indicates where that subject matter is classified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Very important for proper understanding and use; in Definitions, scope-limitation references are listed under 'Limiting references' (example: billiard tables classified elsewhere).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limiting references — precedence
rubrics_metrics.description: A precedence reference states that another place 'takes precedence' when subject matter is classifiable in two places (or aspects covered by different places) and it is desired to classify such subject matter in only one place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precedence references may function as scope-limitation or as classification rules for combination-type subject matter depending on relationship (subsets, overlap, non-overlap). Examples and classification-rule behavior illustrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-limiting references — application-oriented
rubrics_metrics.description: Application-oriented references point from function-oriented places to places where subject matter is covered if specially adapted, used for a particular purpose, or incorporated in a larger system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typically points from a function-oriented place to application examples (examples: lasers → eye surgery, printers, etc.). In Definitions they are listed under 'Application-oriented references'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-limiting references — references out of a residual place
rubrics_metrics.description: References appearing in residual places point to places which provide for the subject matter under consideration (i.e., show where the subject matter actually is covered).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed in Definitions under 'References out of a residual place' with examples (light sources pointing to candles, electric lamps, semiconductor devices).

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-limiting references — informative references
rubrics_metrics.description: Informative references indicate the location of subject matter that could be of interest for searching but which is not within the scope of the classification place where the reference occurs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Informative references usually point from application-oriented places to function-oriented places and are listed in Definitions under 'Informative references'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limiting vs non-limiting references handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Limiting references (scope-limitation and precedence) are included in classification schemes and Definitions; non-limiting references (application-oriented, out of residual place, informative) are being progressively removed from schemes and transferred to Definitions to maintain readability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should consult Definitions for non-limiting reference material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement and interpretation rules for references
rubrics_metrics.description: References are usually placed at the end of the title to which they belong; a reference following a subclass or group title relates to all hierarchically inferior places; when groups are quoted it is usually the most relevant group but not necessarily the only relevant one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where multiple items of subject matter refer to different places, separate by semicolons; where items refer to same place, separate by commas and give classification symbol only at end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notes — scope and precedence
rubrics_metrics.description: Notes define or explain specific words/phrases or the scope of places and may indicate how subject matter is classified; notes apply only to the places concerned and their subdivisions and override any general guidance in case of conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes associated with higher-level places are also reflected in Definitions for impacted subclasses/groups (examples provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of cited classification symbols (in titles/references/notes)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a symbol or contiguous range of symbols is cited in a title, reference or note, the citation comprises not only the symbols explicitly mentioned but their full range of hierarchically inferior subdivisions as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Therefore expressions like 'class and its subclasses' are unnecessary; citation of a subclass includes its main groups and subgroups; examples show how intervals are identified by the hierarchically highest symbol covering the last intended group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indication of changes across editions/versions
rubrics_metrics.description: Text in italics indicates that an entry is new, its file scope has changed, or has been deleted with reference to where subject matter is transferred; version indicators in square brackets show the edition/version when entry was new or changed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deleted group symbols appear with an indication in italics of where the subject matter is transferred; multiple version indicators may be present but only the last is displayed by default.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Definitions to clarify classification scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions provide supplementary information clarifying exact boundaries of classification places; they are recommended to determine scope though they do not change the scope of classification entries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions follow a structured format with a definition statement, explanations of limiting/informative references, interpretation of special classifying rules, and term definitions; Definitions are being expanded progressively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical formulae and graphic illustrations in Definitions/schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: In chemistry-related areas, chemical structural formulae and graphic illustrations are introduced in the scheme or Definitions when necessary to define or interpret scope; additional illustrations are available via hyperlinks in the Internet edition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulae in schemes are used only when necessary to define scope (example: C07D 499/00), while many more examples appear in Definitions for illustration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard expressions and canonical meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: The Guide standardises limited wordings and explains canonical meanings (e.g., 'covered'/'provided for' mean subject matter has characteristics enabling classification in the place).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Users should apply these standard senses when interpreting titles and scheme language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressions indicating residual subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases such as 'not otherwise provided for' mean 'not provided for in any other group in the same subclass or any other subclass'; groups worded '... not provided for in groups...' or 'Other...' cover subject matter not provided for in the stated groups; residual main groups provide for subject matter not covered by other main groups and are usually at the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these expressions to identify residual scope; note that use in a main group title does not expand the scope of the subclass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressions for combination subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Groups that designate subject matter 'covered by more than one of main groups...' provide only for combinations of characteristics not covered as a whole by a single specified group; other wording may provide for combinations or for matter not covered by any group in the specified range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such groups may serve to classify combined features; interpret according to wording and context (example: C05B 21/00).

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'i.e.' and 'e.g.' in titles/Definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: 'i.e.' = equals (the two phrases are equivalent); 'e.g.' = example, does not limit the preceding phrase but illustrates or draws attention to included matter (used to provide typical examples, to show definite inclusion, or indicate matter covered but without dependent subgroup).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided to show usage in group titles and how to interpret inclusion vs illustration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of logical connectors ('and', 'or', 'either...but not both')
rubrics_metrics.description: 'A and B' requires presence of both in same example; 'A or B' implies presence of A or B or both; 'either A or B, but not Both' implies presence of one or the other but not both in same example/embodiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These logical connectives determine how combined features are to be interpreted for classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of 'in general', 'per se', 'specially adapted for'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'In general' indicates things considered for their characteristics disregarding specific application; other standard expressions ('per se', 'specially adapted for') have specialised uses to indicate more precise scope or adaptation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Users should rely on contextual meaning and the Guide's definitions for precise interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and use of 'file scope' of a group
rubrics_metrics.description: File scope = the subject matter which falls within the scope of a group and is not specified in any subgroup indented under it; when a group has no subgroups, scope and file scope are identical; when new subgroups are created, a group's scope remains but its file scope is reduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: File scope represents residual subject matter classified in the group itself but not in its subgroups; important when tracing transfers after revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'essential' characteristic for classification
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'essential' characteristic for classification in a given group is one whose absence would necessitate classification in a different group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determining which characteristics are essential is part of selecting the proper classification place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions and glossary entries as controlling where present
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions given in the Classification override the Guide's Glossary explanations for the places concerned; glossary entries elaborate technical terms used in the Classification but should be read in context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where conflict exists, Definitions associated with specific places take precedence; the glossary is explanatory and not rigid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology and examples for 'combination' and 'subcombination'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Combination' = technical 'thing' consisting of two or more steps or components put together for a purpose (examples: multi-step process, multi-component composition, wheelchair); 'subcombination' = subset of steps/components forming part of entire thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terms are relative (a subcombination may be part of a larger combination); examples illustrate classification implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligatory classification and parallel groups
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Obligatory classification' = the classification necessary to completely represent the invention information of a patent document; 'parallel groups' = groups depending from the same immediate classification place and at same indentation level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obligatory classification must be used to represent all invention information; understanding parallel groups helps in selecting coordinate places.
